subject: electronics
title: Sensor divider: darkness switches the lamp on
objectives: Describe the sensor divider: a fixed resistor and an LDR in series across a 6 V supply, with the output taken across the LDR
Calculate the divided voltage V = 6 V x R_LDR / (R_fixed + R_LDR) at each light level: 1.2 V, 3.0 V, 4.2 V and 5.4 V
Use the 4.5 V threshold to predict when the sensor output switches the lamp on

definitions.meaning: A potential divider whose one resistor is a sensor, here an LDR, so the divided voltage responds to the environment.
A light-dependent resistor whose resistance rises as the light falling on it decreases.
The constant 1 kOhm resistor in series with the LDR; its share of the supply falls as the LDR resistance rises.
Two resistors in series that split the supply voltage in proportion to their resistances.
The output voltage taken across the LDR: 6 V x R_LDR / (R_fixed + R_LDR).
The 4.5 V output level at which the sensor output switches the lamp on.
The 1.2 V across the LDR in bright daylight, when its resistance is only 0.25 kOhm.
The 4.2 V across the LDR at dusk, close to but still below the 4.5 V threshold.
The 5.4 V across the LDR in the dark, when its resistance is 9 kOhm and the lamp lights.

mechanismSteps: Bright daylight, lamp off: the LDR resistance is low at 0.25 kOhm, so it takes only 1.2 V of the 6 V supply and the lamp stays off (s1).
Light falls, output climbs: the LDR resistance steps up to 1 kOhm, equal to the fixed resistor, so the supply splits evenly and the output climbs to 3.0 V (s2).
Dusk, just below the threshold: the LDR resistance steps up to 2.3 kOhm and its share climbs to 4.2 V, still just below the 4.5 V threshold (s3).
Dark, lamp on: the LDR resistance rises to 9 kOhm, it takes 5.4 V, the output crosses the 4.5 V threshold and the lamp lights (s4).
workedExample: Work the climb stage by stage with V = 6 V x R_LDR / (R_fixed + R_LDR). Step 1 (s1): R_LDR = 0.25 kOhm gives 6 x 0.25 / 1.25 = 1.2 V, lamp off. Step 2 (s2): R_LDR = 1 kOhm gives 6 x 1 / 2 = 3.0 V, lamp off. Step 3 (s3): R_LDR = 2.3 kOhm gives about 4.2 V, still below the 4.5 V threshold. Step 4 (s4): R_LDR = 9 kOhm gives 6 x 9 / 10 = 5.4 V, above the threshold, lamp on.

trap.misconception: As it gets darker and the LDR's resistance rises, the voltage across the LDR falls, so the sensor output switches the lamp off.
trap.explanation: The slip: A bigger resistance is imagined to "block" voltage, so the LDR's share is expected to shrink as its resistance grows. The fix: In a series divider each resistor takes a share of the supply in proportion to its resistance, so as the LDR's resistance rises in the dark its share - the output voltage - climbs until it crosses the threshold and switches the lamp on. In class, replay scene 4: freeze the voltmeter at 5.4 V and ask what the reading would be if a bigger resistance really took a smaller share - it would fall below the 4.5 V threshold and the lamp would stay off; it reads 5.4 V, so the bigger resistance must take the bigger share first.
